DDB_G0279167.description: contains 7 BRCT domains Community annotation: Cut genes were originally identified in fission yeast as mutants that lead to cytokinesis in the absense of nuclear division; the name is derived from "cell untimely torn"[1][2]. The genes appear to be a heterogeneous group, most of which have functions required for nuclear division, rather than specifically in the dependence of cytokinesis on successful karyokinesis. Various cut proteins regulate chromosome condensation, assembly of the anaphase promoting complex, sister chromatid decatenation, spindle formation, and, somewhat discordantly, fatty acid synthesis[3]. Two Dicty genes have been named after the original S. pombe cut genes, cut5 (discussed here) and the fatty acid condensing enzyme cutA. Cut5 is widely conserved; in budding yeast it is known as DBP11 and in humans, topoisomerase binding protein 1 (TopBP1). Modern research has identified two roles, one in the initiation of DNA replication, where it interacts with the GINS complex and the other in DNA damage signalling, where it crosslinks the PCNA-like 9-1-1 complex with the DNA damage sensing kinase ATR, resulting in the phosphorylation and activation of the DNA damage effector kinase CHK1. Harry MacWilliams, September 2010 There is more information on the wiki page

DDB_G0270496.description: putative ortholog of H. sapiens AATF, apoptosis-antagonizing transcription factor Community annotation: DDB_G0270496 shows extensive similarities with the "apoptosis antagonizing transcription factor" AATF, which is widely conserved in animals. Under the alternate name Che-1, the gene product has been described as a RNA polymerase II cofactor which associates with the promoters of E2F-activated genes and promotes their transcription under normal conditions. After DNA damage by doxorubicin or ionizing radiation, AATF/Che-1 is phosphorylated by ATM and Chk2, which causes it to dissociate from these promoters and re-associate with those of p53-target genes, as well as p53 itself (see Floridi and Fanciulli, Cell Cycle 6, 804-806 (2007). AATF/Che1 has also been reported to associate with Rb, and to block the Rb-mediated repression of these promoters by HDAC (Fanciulli et al, FASEB Journal 14, 904-912 (2000). DDB_G0270496 is threefold (p<0.004) overexpressed in a Dicty strain in which the retinoblastoma-like gene rblA has been disrupted (Doquang et al, in preparation). Most of the classic E2F target genes are overexpressed in this strain, and it seems possible that AATF/Che1 upregulation contributes to this effect. Harry MacWilliams, September 2009

DDB_G0272758.description: in S. cerevisiae essential for the fidelity of chromosome transmission and component of the RFC complex Community annotation: CTF18 ("chromosome-transmission-fidelity-18") was originally identified as a yeast gene required for the establishment of sister chromatid cohesion. Newer work in both yeasts and mammalian cells shows that CTF18 interacts with DCC1 ("defective in chromosome cohesion-1") and CTF8. Together with the RFC subunits 2-5 they form a complex which shows both PCNA-loading and PCNA-unloading activity in vitro. A recent paper speculates that the complex is required on the lagging strand to allow the replication fork to pass through cohesin rings, which are established around the DNA prior to replication [see Farina et al, Journal of Biological Chemistry 283, 20925-36 (2008), and references cited there]. Dictyostelium has a clear ortholog of DCC1, and a possible ortholog of CTF8 (DDB_G0287975) (E Value 3e-09 by direct comparison with human CTF8). All three of these genes are strongly overexpressed in a Dictyostelium strain in which the retinoblastoma-like gene rblA has been disrupted (CTF18, fivefold; DCC1, 11-fold; CTF8, 25fold) (Doquang et al, in preparation). Most genes with roles in cell cycle progression are overexpressed in this strain. The overexpression factors are similar to those (5 to 15-fold) for other genes whose products are required at the replication fork, such as polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon, and PCNA itself. Harry MacWilliams, November 2009 There is more information on the wiki page
